Our province has about 6 people per square kilometer. Villages are far apart, and some families now drive two hours to the nearest hospital. malthusian-theory-s1.title: From Thomas Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798)
malthusian-theory-s1.html:
"Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. [The food supply] increases only in an arithmetical ratio."

Plain words: left alone, a population multiplies (1, 2, 4, 8, 16), while the food supply only adds a fixed amount each time (1, 2, 3, 4, 5). Malthus argued that hunger, disease and war, which he called checks, would keep population in line with food.

Invented for practice. Family minister of Country E, January 2026:

women-population-change-s2.title: Ravenstein’s laws of migration, summarized
women-population-change-s2.html:
LevlPrep summary of E. G. Ravenstein, "The Laws of Migration" (1885 and 1889), based on British census data:

  • Most migrants move only a short distance.
  • Many move in steps, from village to town to city.
  • People who move long distances usually head for large cities.
  • Each flow of migrants produces a smaller flow back.
  • People from the countryside move more than people from towns.
  • Within their own country, women move more than men; men more often move long distances and abroad.
  • Most migrants are adults, and most move for economic reasons.

migration-causes-s1.title: A migrant describes her move (an invented interview)
migration-causes-s1.html:
Invented for practice. Interview with Ana, 24, who moved from the Northern Hills of Country A to the Capital Region in 2025:

"Two dry summers in a row ruined our maize, and the only work left in my village paid very little. My cousin said the factories in the capital were hiring and paid twice as much. migration-effects-s2.title: A news report from an invented town
migration-effects-s2.html:
Invented for practice. Riverton, a farm town in Country B, 2026:

Twenty years ago, Riverton was losing people. Then a meat-packing plant began hiring workers from abroad. The town’s population has grown by a third, the elementary school has added classrooms and two new grocery stores sell food from home countries. Church services are now held in three languages. At last month’s council meeting, some residents asked for more English classes and help for new families; others asked the national government to lower the number of work visas.
